Coding agents can now help with some of the hardest parts of model optimization: writing complex GPU kernels, performing cross-operator fusions, overlapping computation with communication, and tuning execution across different batch sizes and GPU configurations. For Kimi K3, we used agent-assisted development to build a unified CuTe DSL decode path on the NVIDIA GB300, covering attention, MoE, and communication across 8 or 16 GPUs. The optimizations deliver over 840 tokens/s at batch 1 on 16 NVIDIA GB300 GPUs with DSpark (synthetic AL=6), 1.5–2× higher decode throughput in several tested configurations, and up to 1.8× higher P90 interactivity on the AgentX workload.

Agent-optimized inference code is outpacing our review and maintenance workflow. The manual review process of understanding every line of every kernel, mapping out potential issues, and testing every supported configuration, is very time-consuming work. On the other hand, if we omit this work then we risk shipping buggy software that could fail in production.

There is a clear line-of-sight on how to achieve both goals: we need to change how we organize performance work. Alongside agentic optimization, we need to design systems that allow automatic verification of reliability and performance, and we need to structure the software to enforce isolation and risk minimization by design.

The proposed fast-track model optimization RFC provides a foundation for this approach. Our guiding principle is to decrease review burden while managing risk . To accomplish this, we:

- Isolate changes. Keep optimizations within the model’s code.

- Bound the scope, preserve the core features. Define the supported hardware and workloads but preserve must-have features for production LLM use.

- Validate correctness systematically. Run an established suite of performance and correctness benchmarks to ensure integrity and reliability, and strictly better performance on all supported configurations.

- Scale validation. Let contributors run standard evaluations on their own GPUs and share reproducible results before requesting maintainer attention.

Kimi K3 is our first contribution following this approach. This post covers how we optimized Kimi K3, how we build the confidence needed to ship and maintain those optimizations, and the performance results.

## Table of Contents

- Part 1: Optimizing Kimi K3

- Part 2: Moving Fast and Responsibly

- Part 3: Performance Deep Dive

- What's Next

- Acknowledgements

This contribution introduces a new decode path for Kimi K3 which fuses and replaces almost all operations with customized CuTe DSL kernels, tuned for certain subproblems. It targets NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs with 8 or 16 GPUs, decode batches from 1 to 64, and optional decode context parallelism for long contexts. The GPUs share one NVLink domain with multicast support. For more details, please refer to the PR .

### 1. Tune shapes for the workload

Different batch sizes need different kernel choices. For attention input projections, we use specialized small-matrix kernels at batch sizes 1–2 and split-K kernels at larger batches, which divide the matrix multiplication across more GPU workers. All such projections have been finely tuned to launch well-sized kernels that fully utilize GPU resources and overlap memory reads / communication and compute work as much as possible.

KDA also uses an optimized CuTe DSL decode kernel, with scheduling tuned for the batch size and number of attention heads on each GPU.

For long contexts, decode context parallelism (DCP) splits the KV cache across GPUs. Each GPU computes attention over its local portion, and a tuned fused kernel combines the partial results with v-proj and gating.

### 2. Overlap computation and communication

We fuse attention output projection directly to its all-reduce and the following attention-residual computation. GPU kernels publish partial results into NVLink-accessible buffers, and receiving kernels combine them and continue the computation. Some small-batch configurations fuse the producer and consumer into one kernel. Data exchange is done with a fence-less approach with minimal overhead.

At larger batches, the implementation switches to a two-stage reduction : GPUs first combine assigned portions of the output, then distribute the results. This reduces the data movement between GPUs.

### 3. Improve MoE scheduling and overlap

Although the experts already use tensor parallelism, the baseline computes the full router scores and latent input projection on every GPU. We split these calculations across the TP ranks and combine each rank’s share into one matrix multiplication. The GPUs exchange the results over NVLink. This reduces repeated computation, weight reads, and kernel launches before expert execution begins.

The shared expert runs on a separate stream. Its work overlaps with routing or routed-expert computation, depending on the configuration. The schedule controls how many GPU resources each operation uses, and is carefully tuned to ensure well-balanced parallelism without contention. Details are in experts_runtime .

### 4. Prefetching upcoming weights into cache

In small-batch inference, we are often memory-bound: limited by the speed with which we can load the weights from memory. Some phases cannot fully utilize the available memory bandwidth, such as communication: while this work happens we can run a dedicated kernel on a side stream to ensure that once the communication completes, the weights for the next operation will have a much higher cache hit rate.

Kimi K3 is just one of the first examples. We believe the community can build this together, to bring more models, GPUs, and workloads towards the speed of light.

Different contributors/agents will find different opportunities: a better communication schedule, or a fusion that helps a particular deployment. But if every contribution arrives with different assumptions, incomplete tests, and a benchmark that is hard to reproduce, the validation and maintenance work quickly becomes the bottleneck, or we risk shipping broken code. We need a common way to turn those ideas into improvements that users can rely on for their long-term production use-cases.

This changes what we ask agents to deliver. We should set clear expectations on testing, validations, and requirements for the code agents produce. Agents will construct tests, run comprehensive evaluations and benchmarks, investigate failures, and document the conditions under which the optimization works. Human reviewers still judge the design and the evidence, but they can start from a high-level abstraction, instead of a line-by-line code review.

Building on the proposed fast-track RFC , we organize this work around four principles.

### 1. Isolate changes

Keep model-specific optimizations within the model’s code. This makes the affected paths easier to identify and reduces the blast-radius a reviewer needs to consider.

Isolation also needs to hold at runtime. Reviewers should be able to trace when the optimized path is selected, what state it changes, and how execution returns to the standard path.

This constraint does exclude some optimizations: input preparation, sampling, and KV cache management can cause overhead that isolation excludes. This is a consequence of the design and is largely intentional: these components are all shared among most vLLM deployments, and changing them to optimize for a specific workload risks breaking dozens of other stable vLLM configurations. Work on these components is important, and should involve core maintainers much more closely than the fast-track would permit.

### 2. Bound the scope, but preserve the user’s features

An optimization does not need to improve every deployment to be useful. It can target a particular GPU, parallelism setting, or range of batch sizes. Clear boundaries make the work easier to tune and give us a defined set of configurations to validate.

For K3, the initial hardware validation covers GB300 with TP8 and TP16, decode batches up to 64, speculative decoding with various draft lengths, and decode context-parallel configurations within one NVLink domain.

These boundaries describe where the optimization applies, but not cutting ‘feature coverage’. Production deployment needs fundamental features that make the endpoint useful. Features like full-context serving, temperature sampling, and structured output cannot be “optimized away” or “opt-out”, they are first-class serving features and belong to the validation plan alongside kernel shapes and numerical checks.

### 3. Validate correctness

Kernel tests and model evaluations answer different questions. Kernel tests check numerical results across shapes and input values. Model evaluations check whether the complete execution path preserves the model’s answers. We need both.

The tests must actually exercise the changed code. A small-batch optimization needs evaluation at small batches. An attention kernel change needs long-context coverage. Tests that silently use the standard path provide little evidence about the optimization and are a common trap.

K3 development shows why this matters. Our audit discovered that the compiler moved activation reads ahead of a synchronization wait. The fix restricted that load type to static weights. Such errors can survive simple functional checks and require targeted investigation.

Additionally, long-context and long-generation evaluations such as MRCR and AIME25 surfaced sensitive numerical issues in attention and communication kernels that were not reproducible in standalone kernel tests using mock inputs and/or consistent launch timings.

### 4. Check performance broadly

A headline speedup is a starting point. We also need to know how the change behaves across the workloads it affects. That means sweeping batch sizes, context lengths, and supported parallelism configurations. MoE measurements should include real prompts because expert selection affects which weights are read and how much work can be reused. Pure decode results should also be distinguished from workloads that mix prefill and decode.

Reliable validation also takes GPU time. The related Bring-Your-Own-GPU evaluation RFC proposes standard evaluation images that contributors can run on their own hardware. Reproducible result bundles and submissions linked to GitHub PRs would make the evidence much more accessible. Different evaluation tiers and shared community compute would help expand coverage while managing GPU demand and reducing pressure on project-funded CI.

### Decode performance with DSpark

With DSpark, Kimi K3 reaches 842 tokens per second on 16 NVIDIA GB300 GPUs in the controlled AL=6 benchmark. That is 1.73× faster than stock vLLM with the same speculative decoding setup. Refer to the PR for a full results table.

Setup: TP16, DSpark with seven draft tokens, synthetic acceptance length of 6, DL=7, ISL=1, OSL=1k, batch size 1. TPS measures aggregate decode throughput and excludes prefill.

### Decode performance without speculation

The improvements span across the tested batch range. TP16 retains a 1.62–1.71× gain at batches 16–64 , while TP8 delivers 1.31–1.43× over the same range.

No speculative decoding. Throughput is for the entire TP group.

### Improvement on AgentX

Our optimized Kimi K3 implementation also delivers 1.8× higher P90 interactivity at concurrency 1 on AgentX: 403.2 versus 223.7 tokens/s/user . This compares the optimized run on 16 GB300 GPUs with the earlier vLLM result on 8 GB300 GPUs.

AgentX replays traffic patterns from real coding-agent sessions, including long contexts, multiple conversation turns, tool pauses, parallel subagents, and KV-cache reuse. It preserves these workload patterns while replacing private content with synthetic text, testing the serving system under realistic agent traffic. AgentX methodology .

Ant Group and the vLLM community are open-sourcing Humming, a general-purpose, high-performance kernel library for quantized inference. Humming offers the following features:

- Broad device support : Supports NVIDIA GPU architectures from Turing onward, along with CUDA-compatible devices such as T-Head's Zhenwu 810E.

- Extensive quantization support : A unified architecture supports diverse combinations of weight and activation formats for dense and MoE workloads, covering a wide range of integer and floating-point types, bit widths, and scaling schemes.

- Strong execution performance : Significantly outperforms existing implementations from vLLM Marlin, FlashInfer, and DeepGEMM across many representative workloads.

Repository: github.com/vllm-project/humming

## Background

As models and inference workloads grow, memory capacity, memory bandwidth, and compute costs increasingly constrain deployment. This is especially apparent in MoE models: each token activates only a subset of experts, but the full set of weights still needs to be stored. DeepSeek-V3, for example, has 671 billion parameters, with 37 billion activated per token. Quantization lowers the precision of weights and activations to reduce memory usage and data movement, and can also improve compute efficiency.

Quantization requirements vary across models and GPU generations. Common configurations include WNA16, W8A8, W4A8, and W4A4, where W and A specify weight and activation bit widths, and N denotes a variable weight bit width. Even at the same precision, schemes such as INT4 and NVFP4 differ in numeric format and scaling. Scaling granularity, scale representation, group size, and symmetric or asymmetric quantization further expand the configuration space.

These storage and compute savings only translate into lower latency and higher throughput with efficient kernels. Prefill, decode, and varying MoE expert loads place different demands on compute and memory. Kernels must adapt to these workloads while keeping conversion, dequantization, and scheduling overhead low.

Developing and integrating a dedicated kernel for every combination creates a growing maintenance burden. Each addition can require its own weight preprocessing, kernel selection, framework adapters, and tests. Optimizations must then be carried across multiple implementations.

Humming addresses this problem by separating quantization descriptions from execution choices and composing kernels from shared components.

## General-Purpose Architecture

Humming's execution path has three parts: represent the quantized computation, select configurations for the hardware and workload, and compile a kernel from CUDA components.

### A Unified Quantization Representation

Models exported by different quantization tools vary in numeric format, parameter organization, and weight layout. Humming converts supported export formats into the Humming standard format: a common quantization description with consistently organized weights, scales, zero points, and other tensors.

This representation preserves each scheme's quantization semantics while describing weight format, scaling granularity, scale data type, zero points, and secondary scales as separate parameters. Activations have their own numeric format and quantization settings. These parameters can be combined subject to format and hardware constraints.

For example, groupwise INT4 weights can be paired with BF16 activations. Low-precision floating-point weights with different scaling schemes use the same parameter system. This gives inference frameworks a common interface for models from different sources.

### Tuning and JIT Compilation for Each Workload

The standard format provides a common representation across export formats. Preprocessing then validates parameters, pads dimensions, and repacks these tensors into layouts suited to the target kernel. Humming combines the quantization description with the weight shape, GEMM type, target GPU, and compute options to configure execution.

Three configurations describe the kernel:

- Layer Config describes tensor shapes, data types, quantization parameters, and the target architecture.

- Compute Config specifies the GEMM type and computation options, such as batch invariance and input scale layout.

- Tuning Config selects tile shapes, pipeline stage counts, warp specialization, memory access, and MMA instructions. It also controls concurrency and scheduling; TMA can be configured per tensor.

By default, Humming selects tuning configurations using device-specific heuristics. It can prepare different configurations for ranges of input sizes and dispatch to the appropriate kernel at runtime.

Humming’s unified architecture makes it straightforward to tune execution parameters and select pipelines for different workloads. At small batch sizes, a multistage pipeline using asynchronous copies ( cp.async ) and MMA can outperform a pipeline built around TMA and UMMA. At larger batch sizes, TMA and UMMA can offer better throughput. Humming accommodates both execution paths within the same configuration and component framework, allowing it to select the more effective strategy for each workload.

Together, the three configurations specialize kernels compiled with NVRTC or NVCC. Compiled kernels are cached for reuse. Inference combines the selected kernel with the preprocessed weights and runtime activations.

### Shared CUDA Components Across Formats and Architectures

At the CUDA level, Humming organizes task scheduling, data movement, dequantization and scaling, Tensor Core computation, and output processing into reusable components. It provides standard, warp-specialized, and dedicated UMMA pipelines. These pipelines share compatible components while using the dataflow and synchronization required by each execution strategy.

Each group of components handles a different source of variation:

- Numeric processing handles quantization formats. Decoding and arithmetic components account for bit width, integer or floating-point representation, scales, and zero points. Dequantization and scaling are integrated into the kernel's computation.

- Memory and compute backends handle GPU architectures. Humming selects data movement and Tensor Core implementations for the target architecture, using asynchronous copies, TMA, and multicast where supported.

- Task mapping and scheduling handle dense and MoE workloads. Each GEMM type uses the appropriate scheduling logic. Scaling and bias addition can also be fused into the output stage.

JIT compilation combines these components according to the three configurations and eliminates unused implementation branches. A new format or architecture can therefore be supported by extending the relevant components. Improvements to a shared component benefit compatible configurations, reducing the duplicated development and maintenance of separate specialized kernels.

This CUDA implementation is lightweight and avoids heavyweight kernel framework dependencies, keeping JIT compilation fast as well. In our single W4A16 kernel compilation test on an H200 server with CUDA 13.4, compilation time dropped from 23.35 seconds for CUTLASS with NVCC to 1.82 seconds for Humming with NVCC or 1.88 seconds with NVRTC , with compilation caches disabled. This reduces the cost of preparing kernels for new workloads and makes iterative tuning more practical. Humming also compiles kernels in parallel during model warmup. In our tests, compiling and loading the kernels covering all supported M sizes for a single layer's GEMM takes only about 2–4 seconds , making it practical to prepare multiple specialized kernels before inference.

### Performance Tuning Based on Device Parameters

Humming deeply optimizes kernels using both the GEMM configuration and device parameters. Quantization formats, matrix shapes, GPU instruction support, SM count, shared memory, and register resources all inform execution choices, turning the benefits of low-bit storage into practical inference performance.

Efficient W4A8-MXFP4 inference on existing GPUs. Architectures before Blackwell lack native MXFP4 Tensor Core support, and conventional W4A8-MXFP4 kernels can be limited by dequantization and scaling overhead at larger M. Humming addresses this with a fast MXFP4-to-INT8/FP8 dequantization path that converts MXFP4 weights into a supported compute format within the kernel. In this setting, the path substantially outperforms conventional W4A8 implementations at small M and approaches W8A8 performance at large M. GPUs such as H200 can therefore run high-performance W4A8-MXFP4 kernels while retaining the storage benefits of 4-bit weights.

Dequantization paths matched to each device. The same quantization format can benefit from different implementations across GPUs. Humming selects decoding, numeric conversion, and scaling paths for the device, pairing them with suitable memory access and compute pipelines to reduce instruction and data movement overhead. Shared components make these optimizations reusable across compatible dense and MoE kernels.

Extensive tuning controls with device-specific heuristics. Humming exposes tile shapes, pipeline stage counts, warp specialization, TMA, MMA instructions, CTA concurrency, and Stream-K scheduling. Device-specific heuristics combine GEMM shapes with resource constraints to balance parallelism, data reuse, and pipeline overhead, selecting different execution strategies as input sizes change. Developers can use the default configurations directly or refine them for particular models and deployment scenarios.

## Results

### Broad Device Support

Humming's unified architecture enables broad GPU support. For NVIDIA GPUs, Humming fully supports every architecture from Turing onward, bringing a common quantized computing framework to multiple generations of hardware.

The unified JIT architecture also makes it straightforward to extend Humming to other GPUs compatible with CUDA programming. Humming already fully supports T-Head's Zhenwu 810E, bringing its shared kernels and tuning capabilities to more hardware platforms.

The figure below shows the high-performance activation types supported by Humming on each device: types that can take full advantage of the device's peak compute capabilities. Some types omitted from the figure can still run through other instruction paths. For example, UMMA instructions on the B300 (SM103) no longer support INT8 computation, but earlier MMA instructions can still execute INT8 GEMM, with substantially lower performance.

### Quantization Support

Humming's support for quantization types depends primarily on compatibility between activation and weight types. Its unified quantization representation and kernel architecture allow a wide range of integer and floating-point weight formats to work with activations at different precisions, providing flexible choices for model precision and deployment performance.

The figure below shows the weight and activation type combinations supported by Humming. Rows represent weight types, columns represent activation types, and checks indicate supported combinations. Together with the device support matrix above, it outlines the high-performance quantized computation paths available on each hardware architecture.

Humming also supports a special floating-point format with zero exponent bits, whose representable values match those of symmetric integers at the same bit width. For example, INT8 excluding -128 and float8e0m7 both represent integers from -127 to 127 . Weights in this format have the same activation type compatibility as INT weights of the same bit width. Humming automatically converts eligible symmetric integer weights to this format for faster dequantization.
